To fulfill something means to take something that was expected, required, promised, or hoped for — and actually make it happen, completely and properly.

Think of it this way: before fulfilling happens, there is a gap — a gap between what should happen and what has happened. To fulfill is to close that gap entirely.
The main situations where you use "fulfill"

1. Fulfilling a promise or commitment

When you made a promise and you actually do it — completely — you fulfill it.

"She fulfilled her promise to visit her grandmother every month."
"He made many commitments but fulfilled none of them."

Simply attempting isn't fulfilling. You have to actually deliver on what was said.

2. Fulfilling a duty, role, or responsibility

When a job, role, or responsibility is assigned to you, and you carry it out properly and completely, you fulfill it.

"The soldier fulfilled his duty bravely."
"As a parent, she fulfilled her responsibilities without complaint."
"He was hired as a manager but never fulfilled the role properly."

3. Fulfilling a requirement or condition

When something has rules or criteria that must be met, and you meet all of them, you fulfill those requirements.

"You must fulfill all the eligibility criteria before applying."
"The product did not fulfill the safety standards."
"To graduate, students must fulfill 120 credit hours."

This is very common in formal, academic, and official contexts.

4. Fulfilling a dream, ambition, or potential

This is one of the most emotional and personal uses of the word. When someone achieves what they always dreamed of, or becomes what they were truly capable of becoming, they fulfill that dream or potential.

"After years of struggle, she finally fulfilled her dream of becoming a doctor."
"He had great talent, but he never truly fulfilled his potential."
"Winning the championship fulfilled his lifelong ambition."

5. Fulfilling a need or purpose

When something serves or satisfies a specific need, or achieves its intended purpose, it fulfills that need or purpose.

"This new shelter fulfills a desperate need in the community."
"The device was designed to fulfill a very specific purpose."
"Her new role fulfills her need for creative freedom."

6. Fulfilling an order (in business/commerce)

In business, to fulfill an order means to process it completely — to package the product, ship it, and deliver it to the customer as promised.

"The warehouse fulfills thousands of orders every day."
"Your order has been fulfilled and is on its way."

This is called order fulfillment and it's a very standard term in e-commerce and logistics.
The key nuance — what makes "fulfill" special

The word "fulfill" isn't just about doing something. It carries a deeper meaning: it always implies that something was expected, required, promised, or hoped for beforehand. There had to be an intention, an obligation, or a potential waiting to be realized.

You don't just randomly "fulfill" things. You fulfill something that called for fulfillment.

Also, fulfilling implies completeness. You can't half-fulfill something. Either the promise was kept, the requirement was met, the dream was achieved — or it wasn't. The word leans toward full, proper, satisfying completion.
The related forms you'll constantly encounter

Fulfilled (adjective) — feeling deeply satisfied and content, as if your life or work has real meaning and purpose.

"She felt truly fulfilled as a nurse — the work gave her life meaning."
"He retired feeling fulfilled, having lived exactly as he wanted."

This is about an inner emotional state — a sense of completeness within yourself.

Fulfilling (adjective) — describes an activity, work, or experience that gives you that deep sense of satisfaction and meaning.

"Teaching children is one of the most fulfilling careers."
"He found the volunteer work deeply fulfilling."

Unfulfilled (adjective) — when something that should have been fulfilled wasn't. It describes either unmet expectations or a person who feels their potential hasn't been realized.

"She died with many unfulfilled dreams."
"He felt restless and unfulfilled in his job."

Fulfillment (noun) — the act or state of fulfilling something, or the feeling of deep personal satisfaction.

"The fulfillment of his contract was delayed."
"She found great fulfillment in raising her children."

These words overlap with "fulfill," but each has its own shade of meaning:

Fulfill vs. Complete
"Complete" just means to finish something — to bring it to its end. "Fulfill" adds the layer of meeting an expectation, promise, or requirement. You can complete a task mechanically; fulfilling it means it was done in a way that fully satisfied what was needed.

"He completed the report." (He finished it.)
"He fulfilled the requirements of the job." (He met all that was expected of him.)

Fulfill vs. Achieve
"Achieve" focuses on reaching a goal through your own effort. "Fulfill" leans more toward living up to something that was already expected, required, or promised — whether by yourself or by others.

"She achieved great success." (She worked hard and got there.)
"She fulfilled her potential." (She became what she was always capable of being.)

Fulfill vs. Satisfy
"Satisfy" means to meet a need or desire adequately. "Fulfill" is stronger — it implies a deeper, more complete meeting of something, often with a sense of purpose or obligation attached.

"This snack satisfies my hunger." (It's enough.)
"This career fulfills my need for meaningful work." (It meets it deeply and completely.)

Fulfill vs. Honor
"Honor" is specifically used for promises and commitments in a formal or respectful sense. "Fulfill" is broader and can apply to promises, duties, dreams, requirements, and more.

"She honored her agreement with the client."
"She fulfilled her promise, her duty, and her dream." (Wider range)
A quick mental test to know when to use "fulfill"

Ask yourself: Was there something expected, required, promised, or hoped for — and did it actually happen fully?

If yes — that's fulfill.

A soldier does their duty → fulfills their duty.
A student meets all the graduation requirements → fulfills the requirements.
A person achieves the dream they always had → fulfills their dream.
A product serves the purpose it was designed for → fulfills its purpose.
A person feels deeply satisfied with their life → feels fulfilled.
